  16. Full-screen apps often switch to the alternate screen buffer.
  17. Changed cells are marked dirty so they will be redrawn.
  18. Redraws are batched and usually synced to the display's refresh rate.
  19. The renderer goes through the dirty rows of the grid.
  20. Neighbouring cells with the same style are grouped into runs.
  21. Each run is sent through a text shaper, such as HarfBuzz.
  22. Shaping turns code points into glyph IDs and handles ligatures.
  23. Font fallback finds another font when the main font lacks a glyph.
  24. A rasterizer, such as FreeType or Core Text, turns glyph outlines into bitmaps.
  25. Antialiasing smooths glyph edges using partial coverage values.
  26. Rendered glyphs are cached in a texture atlas on the GPU.
  27. Cell backgrounds are drawn first, as filled rectangles.
  28. Glyph quads are drawn next, sampling from the atlas.
  29. Foreground color is applied per glyph using the cell's attributes.
  30. Underline, strikethrough and undercurl are drawn as extra shapes.
  31. Box-drawing and block characters are often drawn by the terminal's own code, so they line up exactly.
  32. Color emoji come from bitmap or color-layer font tables.
  33. The cursor is drawn last, as a block, bar or underline.
  34. Selection highlighting inverts or tints the selected cells.
  35. The finished frame is presented through OpenGL, Metal, Vulkan or a 2D API.
  36. Resizing the window changes the grid size and sends SIGWINCH to the program.
  37. The program redraws its output to fit the new dimensions.
  38. Synchronized-update modes stop a half-drawn frame from flickering.
  39. Older terminals drew straight to the screen with no GPU.
  40. Underneath it all, it's still just a stream of bytes turned into a grid.
